title: Anybody Headed Down Today?
intro: Sunday morning, and Priya's out front of Middle Brook Cafe in Jefferson, checking her phone every few minutes between customers.
smallTalk: Priya's kid has a showcase in the city tonight. Half the village knows and it isn't even nine.
Walt's truck is sitting on J&H's lot with the hood up.
The trail's dry the whole way to Hobart this week. Somebody's already walked it this morning.
Tops finally got the good peaches in.
This has been the soggiest summer anybody up here can remember, and everybody's got an opinion about it.
Nice to see everybody pitching in for Priya's kid.
Somebody's fixing up the space under Stamford Coffee. Nobody will say what it is.
Stamford Coffee's got a record on and a whole shelf of coffee makers lined up like a parade. Go look, it's worth the trip on its own.
If you're late getting home, the self-serve fridge at Stamford Coffee has dinner in it.
80 Main's got the Catskills sweaters in again. I'm going to go and look at them.

items.name: Priya's costume bag
items.blurb: Half a dance costume, sequins and all.

items.name: Jess R.'s jumper cables
items.blurb: Red and black, coiled neat, out of the back of her truck.

lines: He sent a photo from the stage door. Sequins and all.
Thank you.
Good. He'll be glad of you.
His battery's dead? Poor Walt. He'll be more bothered about the truck than about my bag.
Walt's up at J&H, on the corner. He'll be out front with the truck.
My kid's in a dance showcase in the city tonight, and half his costume is still on our kitchen table. It's in this bag.
I'm on the register at Middle Brook till four, and it's three hours down. He needs it by five, when they call them in.
Walt goes down every other Sunday. He's up at J&H with the truck — would you take it to him?
Cables. Now I want a car parked alongside with a good battery in it, running ten minutes.
Ask a Jess. It's usually one of them who does this for me.
Still dead. I need cables, and a car with a good battery in it parked alongside.
Two Jesses in Stamford, one down in Hobart, one somewhere round this village.
Priya's kid's costume? Leave it on the seat — it's going down with me. Every other Sunday, and today's a Sunday.
Battery's dead, though. I need a jump and I've left my cables at home.
Find me somebody who can give me one. It's usually a Jess — there's four of them between here and Hobart, and I've never once picked the right one first.
Morning. Battery's dead. I need a jump and I've left my cables at home.
Walt got his jump, then. Jess R. will want those cables back.
You've got Jess R.'s cables, I see. She'd lend them to anyone.
The south end of the trail, where the old rail bed starts. She'll have a pack on.
Walt's battery again.
Jess R. went by here at eight with a pack on, headed for the trail. She keeps cables in the back of that truck of hers.
Morning. Nothing doing till the mail comes.
He got a jump, then. I'll get the cables back off him sometime.
Go on, then. I've got eleven miles to walk.
Cables? I've a set in the back of the truck. Here.
Leave them with Walt when you're done — he's good for them.

effects.toast: You've got Jess R.'s jumper cables.

lines: Eleven miles of old rail bed to Hobart and not one hill on it. I'll be there by lunch.
If you've never walked it, walk it. You can hear the creek most of the way.
The truck's away, then. Ten minutes, like I said.
Walt got a jump, then. That's all that truck ever wants.
That's the cables. Now the car.
Cables, and a car with a good battery in it. Ten minutes, running.
Walt's green pickup? I've had my head under that hood. Cables on their own won't start it.
He needs a car with a good battery parked next to his, running, ten minutes at least.
This is the best spot in Hobart. The water does all the talking.
Ten minutes and it started. That's all it was.
Sit tight. It wants a good ten minutes.
You've got cables. My wagon's over at the gas station and it starts first turn every time.
Come on, then. I'm not doing anything today.
Walt's battery? I'd bring the wagon over now, only I've no cables either.
Mine went off in a car I sold in April.
Coffee on the patio and nothing I have to do. It's a good morning for it.
That's my wagon over at the gas station. I walked across.
Tell me that bag made it to the stage door.
Those are Jess R.'s. She'll not have asked for them back yet.
Walt needs a jump? Then it's a Jess he wants.

Walt's your man, up at J&H in Jefferson. Every other Sunday, regular as the mail.

Glad it worked out. Come by Cellar Door for a tasting sometime.
You got them off Jess R., then. Good.
Walt needs a jump? My truck's been in the shop two weeks, or I'd go up myself.
Jess T. had her own hood up half of last winter and never once called anyone. She's over by the bridge most mornings.
Priya's costume run? Word travels. Not me today — my truck's in the shop.
Walt goes down every other Sunday. He's the one to ask.
Welcome — pull up a seat on the bench anytime.
If you're headed up toward Jefferson, say hello to Priya at Middle Brook.
So Walt got away after all. Tell Priya's kid break a leg from all of us in here.
Somebody came in saying Walt's battery is dead. He'll be fine — nobody's stuck long around here.
Downstairs? I've heard four different things this week and I believe none of them.

Nobody knows and everybody's got a theory.
I say oysters. The wine nights in here fill right up.
Whoever it is, they've picked a lovely spot. Coffee upstairs, sweaters next door.
Don't mind me, I'm deciding between two sweaters and losing.
You've noticed the work going on under the coffee shop? Whole town's noticed. Nobody's got the answer, which hasn't slowed anybody down.

Red to red, black on the bracket. Now leave it running.

steps.toast: Episode complete — new story next week

lines: Taped inside the door: "The truck on the lot is Walt's. He's waiting on a jump."
Pinned to the board by the door: somebody's asking if anybody's headed down to the city tonight. Two people have written "ask Walt" underneath, in two different pens.
Down the side of the coffee shop, a low window right at the ground, with brown paper and a sheet of plywood over it from the inside. Somebody's at work behind it — you can hear a saw going.
Not a word written on any of it. Everybody who walks past leans in anyway.
